decks.title: Arithmetic Progression — Part 1: Common difference and the general term
goals: Decide whether a sequence is an arithmetic progression and find its common difference
Write the general (nth) term of an AP and find any term
Find which term a given number is, and the number of terms of a finite AP
Find an AP from two conditions, and work with three terms in AP

slides.heading: Arithmetic Progression, Part 1
slides.body_md: An **arithmetic progression** (AP) grows or shrinks by the same amount at every step. Plotted against the term number, its terms lie on a straight line.

visual.alt: The terms 3, 8, 13, 18 and 23 plotted against their term numbers 1 to 5: the points lie on a straight line that rises by 5 for every step to the right.
visual.caption: Each step adds the same $5$: the terms of an AP lie on a straight line.

slides.narration: Welcome to arithmetic progressions. Look at the numbers three, eight, thirteen, eighteen and twenty three. Each one is five more than the one before. Plot them against their positions and they sit on a straight line. In this part you will learn to recognise such sequences and to find any term without listing them all.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Decide whether a sequence is an **AP** and find its **common difference** $d$
Write the **general term** $T_n$ and find any term
Find **which term** a number is, and **how many terms** an AP has
Find an AP from **two conditions**; handle **three terms in AP**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. First we see what makes a sequence an arithmetic progression. Then we build a formula for any term. We use it to find term numbers and to count terms, and finally we find a whole progression from two facts about it.

slides.heading: What is an arithmetic progression?
slides.body_md: A **sequence** is a list of numbers in order: $T_1, T_2, T_3, \ldots$ It is an **AP** if every term after the first is the term before it plus a fixed number $d$, the **common difference**.

visual.alt: Table of four sequences and their differences: 4, 11, 18, 25 has differences 7, 7, 7 and is an AP; 30, 24, 18, 12 has differences minus 6 each time and is an AP; 5, 5, 5, 5 has differences 0 and is an AP; 2, 3, 5, 8 has differences 1, 2, 3 and is not an AP.
visual.caption: Same difference every time: an AP. Changing differences: not an AP.

math: T_{n+1} - T_n = d \text{ for every } n
slides.narration: A sequence is simply a list of numbers in a definite order. It is an arithmetic progression when you always add the same number to get from one term to the next. That fixed number is the common difference. The table checks four sequences. Three of them have the same difference every time. The last does not, so it is not an arithmetic progression.

slides.heading: The common difference
slides.body_md: Find $d$ as **a term minus the term before it**: $d = T_2 - T_1$. It can be positive (rising terms), negative (falling terms), zero (constant terms), or a fraction or decimal.

visual.alt: Two arithmetic progressions plotted against term number: 2, 5.5, 9, 12.5, 16 rising by 3.5 each step, and 20, 17.5, 15, 12.5, 10 falling by 2.5 each step; both have 12.5 as their fourth term.
visual.caption: Positive $d$: the terms rise. Negative $d$: they fall.

slides.narration: To find the common difference, always take a term minus the one before it, never the other way round. If the difference is positive, the terms rise; if it is negative, they fall; if it is zero, every term is the same. The graph shows one progression rising by three and a half, and another falling by two and a half.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is it an AP?
bullets: **Step 1 —** work out every difference, later term minus earlier term (table).
**Answer —** (i) is an AP with $d = 6$ and (iii) with $d = -2.5$; (ii) and (iv) are not APs.

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: 11, 17, 23, 29 has differences 6, 6, 6, an AP; 2, 6, 18, 54 has differences 4, 12, 36, not an AP; minus 1.5, minus 4, minus 6.5, minus 9 has differences minus 2.5 each time, an AP; 1, 4, 9, 16 has differences 3, 5, 7, not an AP.
visual.caption: Work out every difference before deciding.

slides.narration: Work out every difference, not just the first one. In list one each step adds six. In list two the steps are four, twelve and thirty six, so it is not an arithmetic progression. In list three each step subtracts two and a half. In list four the steps are three, five and seven, so the differences change.

slides.heading: Quick check: the common difference
slides.body_md: Subtract each term from the one after it.
slides.narration: Take the second term minus the first term. Be careful with the minus signs.

slides.heading: The general term
slides.body_md: Start at $a$ and add $d$ once for each step. To reach the $n$th term you take $n - 1$ steps, so the **general term** (the $n$th term) is

visual.alt: Table building the general term: term 1 is a, term 2 is a plus d, term 3 is a plus 2 d, term 4 is a plus 3 d, so term n is a plus n minus 1 times d; for 6, 10, 14 this gives 6, 10, 14, 18 and in general 4 n plus 2.
visual.caption: To reach the $n$th term you add $d$ exactly $n - 1$ times.

slides.narration: Here is the key formula. The first term is a. The second is a plus d, the third is a plus two d, and so on. To reach the nth term you take one step fewer than n, so the nth term is a plus n minus one, times d. Some books write it as t n or a n; in this course we write capital T n.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the nth term
slides.body_md: For the AP $13, 8, 3, \ldots$ write the general term and find the $18$th term.

visual.alt: Terms of 13, 8, 3 and so on plotted against n: the points lie on the falling line T n equals 18 minus 5 n, which reaches minus 72 at n equals 18.
visual.caption: The $18$th term lies on the same line: $T_{18} = -72$.

slides.narration: The first term is thirteen and each step subtracts five, so the common difference is minus five. Substituting, the nth term simplifies to eighteen minus five n. Put n equal to eighteen to get minus seventy two. A quick check: n equal to three gives three, which is the third term.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: which term is it?
slides.body_md: In the AP $4.5, 7, 9.5, \ldots$ which term is $57$? Is $60$ a term?
bullets: **Answer —** $n = 23.2$ is not a whole number, so $60$ is **not** a term.

nodes.label: No: it is not a term

visual.alt: Flow chart for deciding whether a number is a term: write a plus n minus 1 times d equal to the number, solve for n, and ask whether n is a positive whole number; if yes it is the nth term, if not it is not a term of the progression.
visual.caption: A term number must be a positive whole number.

slides.narration: Put the formula for the nth term equal to the given number and solve for n. For fifty seven we get n equals twenty two, a whole number, so fifty seven is the twenty second term. For sixty, n minus one is twenty two point two, so n is not a whole number, and sixty is not a term at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: a far-away term
slides.body_md: Use $T_n = a + (n - 1)d$.
slides.narration: Find the first term and the common difference, then take fifteen steps from the first term.

slides.heading: Counting terms; terms from the end
slides.body_md: For a finite AP with last term $l$: solve $a + (n - 1)d = l$ to count the terms. Read backwards, the AP starts at $l$ with common difference $-d$, so the $m$th term from the end is $l - (m - 1)d$.

visual.alt: Table for the progression 9, 16, 23 up to 352: counted from the start the first three terms are 9, 16 and 23; counted from the end they are 352, 345 and 338; the mth term from the end is 352 minus m minus 1 times 7.
visual.caption: Read backwards, an AP is still an AP, with common difference $-d$.

math: m\text{th term from the end} = l - (m - 1)d
slides.narration: A finite progression stops at a last term, usually called l. To count its terms, find which term l is. To find a term counted from the end, turn the progression round: it now starts at l and goes down by d each step. So the mth term from the end is l minus m minus one, times d.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: counting terms
slides.body_md: How many terms does the AP $9, 16, 23, \ldots, 352$ have? Find its $10$th term from the end.
bullets: **Check —** it is the $41$st term from the start: $T_{41} = 9 + 40 \times 7 = 289$.
**Answer —** $50$ terms; the $10$th term from the end is $289$.

visual.alt: The progression 9, 16, 23 up to 352 plotted against term number: a rising line from the point (1, 9) to the point (50, 352), with the 10th term from the end, 289, marked at n equals 41.
visual.caption: The $10$th term from the end is the $50 - 10 + 1 = 41$st term.

slides.narration: Solve nine plus n minus one times seven equals three hundred and fifty two. That gives n equals fifty. For the tenth term from the end, start at three hundred and fifty two and take nine steps down of seven, giving two hundred and eighty nine. As a check, it is the forty first term from the start.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: an AP from two terms
slides.body_md: The $5$th term of an AP is $31$ and the $14$th term is $-5$. Find the AP and its $30$th term.

visual.alt: A falling line through the points (5, 31) and (14, minus 5), continued back to the first term 47 at n equals 1 and on to minus 69 at n equals 30.
visual.caption: Two terms fix the line, and so the whole AP.

slides.narration: Write both terms in terms of a and d and subtract. Between the fifth and fourteenth terms there are nine steps, and the value falls by thirty six, so d is minus four. Going back four steps from thirty one gives the first term, forty seven. The thirtieth term is then minus sixty nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: which term?
slides.body_md: Solve $a + (n - 1)d = 171$.
slides.narration: Subtract the first term, divide by the common difference, and remember to add one.

slides.heading: Three terms in AP
slides.body_md: Three unknown terms in AP are best written $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$: their sum is simply $3a$. Three numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ are in AP exactly when the middle one is the average of the others: $2b = a + c$.

rows: $a$, $b$, $c$ in AP exactly when $2b = a + c$

visual.alt: Table of two ideas for three terms in an arithmetic progression: write them as a minus d, a, a plus d so that their sum is 3 a; and a, b, c are in AP exactly when 2 b equals a plus c, which for 5 m plus 2, 4 m plus 7 and 2 m plus 15 gives m equals 3.
visual.caption: Symmetric terms make the sum simple.

slides.narration: When a question is about three numbers in arithmetic progression, call them a minus d, a and a plus d. The d cancels in the sum, so the sum gives a at once. And three numbers are in arithmetic progression exactly when twice the middle one equals the sum of the outer two.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: three numbers
slides.body_md: Three numbers in AP have sum $36$ and product $1428$. Find them.
bullets: **Answer —** the numbers are $7, 12, 17$ (with $d = -5$, the same numbers in reverse order).

visual.alt: Bar chart of the three numbers 7, 12 and 17: each bar is 5 taller than the one before, and the middle bar, 12, is the average of the other two.
visual.caption: Equal steps of $5$ either side of the middle number $12$.

slides.narration: Write the numbers as a minus d, a and a plus d. Their sum is three a, which is thirty six, so a is twelve. The product becomes twelve times one hundred and forty four minus d squared. That equals one thousand four hundred and twenty eight, so d squared is twenty five, and the numbers are seven, twelve and seventeen.

slides.heading: Worked example 7: a stack of chairs
slides.body_md: One imagined plastic chair is $82$ cm tall, and each extra chair stacked on it adds $4$ cm. (a) How tall is a stack of $15$ chairs? (b) How many chairs make a stack $150$ cm tall?

visual.alt: Height of a stack of imagined plastic chairs against the number of chairs: 82 centimetres for one chair, rising 4 centimetres per chair, 138 centimetres for 15 chairs and 150 centimetres for 18 chairs.
visual.caption: Each extra chair adds the same $4$ cm.

slides.narration: The heights of the stacks go up by four centimetres for each extra chair, so they form an arithmetic progression starting at eighty two. Fifteen chairs give the fifteenth term, one hundred and thirty eight centimetres. For one hundred and fifty centimetres, solve for n: eighteen chairs.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Think about what happens to each difference.
slides.narration: If you subtract the same number from two neighbouring terms, what happens to their difference?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: AP: each term $=$ previous term $+ d$; $d = T_2 - T_1$
Which term or how many terms: solve $a + (n - 1)d = $ value; $n$ must be a positive whole number
Three terms: $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$; or $2b = a + c$

rows: $d = T_2 - T_1$ (a term minus the one before it)

visual.alt: Summary table for part 1: in an arithmetic progression each term is the previous term plus d; d is a term minus the one before; the general term is a plus n minus 1 times d; count terms by solving for n; the mth term from the end is l minus m minus 1 times d; three terms can be taken as a minus d, a, a plus d.
visual.caption: Part 1 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. In an arithmetic progression you add the same common difference each time. The nth term is a plus n minus one, times d. To find which term a number is, solve for n and check that it is a positive whole number. Count from the end by turning the progression round. And take three terms as a minus d, a and a plus d.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Find a term (2 marks):** $a$ and $d$ identified 1 + correct term 1
**Which term / is it a term (2–3 marks):** equation 1 + solving 1 + conclusion 1
**AP from two conditions (3–4 marks):** each equation 1 + solving + the AP
**Mistake:** $d = T_1 - T_2$ (wrong order) gives the wrong sign
**Mistake:** forgetting that $n$ must be a positive whole number
slides.narration: Always write a and d first: that usually earns the first mark. Show the equation when you find a term number, and state your conclusion in words. Watch the order when you subtract: a term minus the one before. Use n minus one, not n, in the formula. And a term number must be a positive whole number.

decks.title: Arithmetic Progression — Part 2: Sum of the first n terms and applications
goals: Find the sum of the first n terms of an AP with either form of the sum formula
Find the number of terms when the sum is given
Find terms from a rule for the sum, and the sum of a block of terms
Solve real-life problems such as savings and instalments that change by a fixed amount

slides.heading: Arithmetic Progression, Part 2
slides.body_md: Add the terms of an AP one after another and the running totals grow faster and faster. One formula gives any total at once.

visual.alt: Running totals of 4, 7, 10, 13 and so on plotted against the number of terms: 4, 11, 21, 34, 50 and 69. The points lie on a curve that bends upwards, not on a straight line.
visual.caption: The terms rise steadily, so the totals grow faster and faster.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Here we add the terms of an arithmetic progression. The running totals of four, seven, ten, thirteen and so on are four, eleven, twenty one, thirty four, and they grow faster and faster. You will learn a formula that gives any total at once, and use it in real problems.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find $S_n$, the **sum of the first $n$ terms**, in two ways
Find **how many terms** give a given sum
Get **terms from sums**, and add a **block of terms**
slides.narration: These are your goals for part two. We derive the sum formula and use both of its forms. Then we work backwards from a sum to the number of terms, find terms from a rule for the sum, and finally solve everyday problems about savings and instalments.

slides.heading: Adding by pairing
slides.body_md: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: every column gives first term $+$ last term. With $n$ columns, $2S_n = n(a + l)$.

visual.alt: Table writing the sum 4 plus 7 plus 10 plus 13 plus 16 plus 19 forwards and backwards: each column adds up to 23, so twice the sum is 6 times 23, which is 138, and the sum is 69.
visual.caption: Each column adds up to first term $+$ last term, so $S = \dfrac{6}{2}(4 + 19) = 69$.

slides.narration: Here is a neat trick. Write the sum forwards, then backwards underneath, and add the columns. Each column adds up to the same total, the first term plus the last. With six columns, twice the sum is six times twenty three. So the sum is half of that, sixty nine. In general, the sum is n over two, times the first term plus the last term.

slides.heading: The sum formula in two forms
slides.body_md: Since $l = a + (n - 1)d$, the pairing formula can be written without $l$:

visual.alt: Flow chart for choosing a sum formula: if a, d and n are known use n over 2 times 2 a plus n minus 1 times d; if a, the last term l and n are known use n over 2 times a plus l; if a, d and l are known, first find n, then use n over 2 times a plus l.
visual.caption: Two forms of the same formula.

slides.narration: The last term is a plus n minus one times d. Put that into the pairing formula and you get the first form: n over two, times two a plus n minus one times d. Use it when you know a, d and n. Use the second form, n over two times a plus l, when you know the first and last terms.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a direct sum
slides.body_md: Find the sum of the first $16$ terms of the AP $40, 36, 32, \ldots$

visual.alt: Bar chart of the first 16 terms of 40, 36, 32 and so on: the bars fall by 4 each time, from 40 down to 0 at the 11th term and then below the axis to minus 20 at the 16th term.
visual.caption: The negative terms at the end cancel part of the total: $S_{16} = 160$.

slides.narration: Here a is forty, d is minus four and n is sixteen. Two a is eighty, and fifteen times minus four is minus sixty, so the bracket is twenty. Eight times twenty is one hundred and sixty. The bar chart shows why the sum is small: the last few terms are negative and cancel part of the total.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: first and last terms

visual.alt: The terms of minus 8, minus 3, 2, 7 and so on plotted against n: a rising line from (1, minus 8) to (25, 112). The sum is 25 times the average of these two end values, 52.
visual.caption: Sum $=$ number of terms $\times$ average of first and last: $25 \times 52 = 1300$.

slides.narration: The common difference is five and the last term is one hundred and twelve. First count the terms: n is twenty five. Now the second form is quickest: twenty five over two, times minus eight plus one hundred and twelve, which is twelve and a half times one hundred and four, or one thousand three hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: which formula?
slides.body_md: Think of pairing first and last terms.
slides.narration: Each pair adds up to the first term plus the last term. How many pairs are there?

slides.heading: Finding n when the sum is given
slides.body_md: Put the sum formula equal to the given sum. This gives a **quadratic in $n$**; keep only roots that are positive whole numbers.

nodes.label: Set it equal to the given sum
Rearrange to a quadratic in $n$ and solve

visual.alt: Flow chart for finding the number of terms from a given sum: write S n using a and d, set it equal to the sum, rearrange to a quadratic in n and solve, keep only positive whole-number roots, and check by working out the sum.
visual.caption: A number of terms must be a positive whole number.

slides.narration: Sometimes the sum is given and you must find how many terms were added. Put the sum formula equal to the given sum. Because the formula has n times a bracket containing n, you get a quadratic. Solve it, and keep only roots that are positive whole numbers. Then check by working out the sum.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: how many terms?
slides.body_md: How many terms of the AP $25, 22, 19, \ldots$ must be taken so that their sum is $116$?
bullets: **Answer —** $n$ must be a whole number, so $n = 8$. Check: $S_8 = 4(50 - 21) = 116$.

visual.alt: Graph of the sum of the first n terms of 25, 22, 19 and so on: it rises to just above 117 and falls again. The horizontal line at 116 meets it at n equals 8 and again at a fraction between 9 and 10, which is not a whole number of terms.
visual.caption: Only $n = 8$ is a whole number of terms; $n = \dfrac{29}{3}$ is rejected.

slides.narration: Write the sum with a equal to twenty five and d equal to minus three, and set it equal to one hundred and sixteen. That gives a quadratic, which factorises. The roots are eight and twenty nine thirds. A number of terms must be a whole number, so the answer is eight. The graph shows the sum reaching one hundred and sixteen at n equals eight.

slides.heading: Quick check: a sum
slides.body_md: Use $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]$.
slides.narration: Find the common difference first, then substitute into the first form of the sum formula.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a block of terms
slides.body_md: Find the sum of the terms from the $11$th to the $30$th of the AP $6, 11, 16, \ldots$

visual.alt: Bar chart of the first 30 terms of 6, 11, 16 and so on, in two colours: the first ten bars, from 6 to 51, and the next twenty bars, from 56 to 151, whose total is wanted.
visual.caption: The wanted part is the whole $S_{30}$ minus the first part $S_{10}$.

slides.narration: There are two good ways. Subtract the sum of the first ten terms from the sum of the first thirty. Or treat the block as its own progression of twenty terms, from the eleventh term, fifty six, to the thirtieth, one hundred and fifty one, and use the pairing formula. Both give two thousand and seventy.

slides.heading: From the sum back to the terms
slides.body_md: If a rule for $S_n$ is given: $T_1 = S_1$, and for $n \ge 2$ the $n$th term is what the $n$th addition contributes.

visual.alt: Table for the sum rule S n equals 7 n minus n squared: the sums for n equals 1 to 5 are 6, 10, 12, 12 and 10, and the terms found by subtracting consecutive sums are 6, 4, 2, 0 and minus 2, an arithmetic progression with common difference minus 2.
visual.caption: Subtracting consecutive sums gives the terms $6, 4, 2, 0, -2, \ldots$: $d = -2$.

slides.narration: Sometimes you are given a rule for the sum instead of the terms. The first term is just the first sum. After that, each term is the difference between consecutive sums, because the nth sum is the previous sum plus the nth term. For the rule seven n minus n squared, the terms are six, four, two, zero and so on.

slides.heading: Quick check: true or false?
slides.body_md: Try a simple AP such as $1, 2, 3, 4$.
slides.narration: Add the first two terms, then the first four terms. Did the sum double?

slides.heading: Worked example 5: repaying a loan
slides.body_md: Harpreet, who runs an imagined tailoring shop in Amritsar, repays an interest-free loan of ₹$30{,}000$ in monthly instalments: ₹$750$ in the first month and ₹$150$ more each month. How many instalments does she pay, and what is the last one?

visual.alt: Bar chart of 16 monthly instalments rising by 150 rupees each month, from 750 rupees in month 1 to 3000 rupees in month 16; together they add up to 30000 rupees.
visual.caption: Sixteen instalments, each ₹$150$ more than the last, add up to ₹$30{,}000$.

slides.narration: The instalments form an arithmetic progression with first term seven hundred and fifty and common difference one hundred and fifty. Their sum must be thirty thousand. That gives a quadratic, which factorises with roots sixteen and minus twenty five. So she pays sixteen instalments, and the last is three thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a rolling trolley
slides.body_md: An imagined trolley rolling down a ramp travels $4$ cm in the first second, $12$ cm in the second, $20$ cm in the third, and so on. (a) How far does it travel in the $10$th second? (b) How far does it travel in the first $10$ seconds?
bullets: **Step 1 —** distances in each second form an AP with $a = 4$, $d = 8$.

visual.alt: Total distance travelled by the imagined trolley against time: 4 centimetres after 1 second, 16 after 2 seconds, 36 after 3 seconds and 400 after 10 seconds, on the curve 4 n squared.
visual.caption: Distances in each second form an AP; the running totals are $4n^2$.

slides.narration: The distances covered in each second go up by eight centimetres, so they form an arithmetic progression. In the tenth second the trolley covers seventy six centimetres. In the first ten seconds altogether it covers four hundred centimetres. The graph shows the total distance growing like four times the square of the time.

slides.heading: Choosing the right formula
slides.body_md: Read what is **given** and what is **asked**, then choose:

visual.alt: Table for choosing a method: a term from a, d and n uses a plus n minus 1 times d; which term solves that equal to the value; a sum uses either sum formula; the number of terms from a sum needs a quadratic in n; a term from a sum rule uses S n minus S n minus 1.
visual.caption: Read the question for what is given and what is asked.

slides.narration: In the exam, first write down what you are given and what you are asked. A single term needs the nth term formula. A sum needs one of the two sum formulas. If the sum is given and n is wanted, expect a quadratic. And if you are given a rule for the sum, subtract consecutive sums to get the terms.

slides.heading: Quick check: an application
slides.body_md: Identify $a$, $d$ and $n$ first.
slides.narration: Which day is it, and how many steps of the common difference is that from the first day?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: $n$ from a sum: quadratic; keep positive whole numbers

rows: quadratic in $n$; keep positive whole numbers
identify $a$, $d$, $n$; watch the units and the first term

visual.alt: Summary table for part 2: the two sum formulas; n from a given sum by a quadratic, keeping positive whole numbers; the sum of a block of terms as S n minus S m; terms from sums; and in applications identify a, d and n and watch units and the first term.
visual.caption: Part 2 on one card.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The sum of the first n terms has two forms, one with d and one with the last term. If the sum is given, solve a quadratic for n. A block of terms is a difference of two sums. Terms come from sums by subtraction. And in applications, identify a, d and n carefully.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Sum of n terms (2 marks):** correct form with $a$, $d$, $n$ 1 + value 1
**Number of terms from a sum (3–4 marks):** equation 1 + quadratic 1 + roots 1 + rejecting a root with a reason 1
**Application (10-mark part):** $a$, $d$ identified + formula + answer with units
**Mistake:** $(n - 1)$ replaced by $n$ in the sum formula
**Mistake:** keeping a negative or fractional value of $n$
slides.narration: Write the formula before substituting: the method mark is for the correct form. When n is unknown, show the quadratic and both roots, then say why you reject one. In word problems state a and d in words, and give units in the answer. Common slips are using n instead of n minus one, and forgetting to halve.

notes.title: Arithmetic Progression — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Sequences and arithmetic progressions
sections.body_md:
- A **sequence** is a list of numbers in a definite order: $T_1, T_2, T_3, \ldots$ ($T_n$ is the $n$th term).
- An **arithmetic progression (AP)** is a sequence in which each term after the first is obtained by adding a fixed number $d$, the **common difference**, to the term before it.
- $d = T_2 - T_1 = T_3 - T_2 = \cdots$: always a term **minus the one before it**.
- $d > 0$: rising terms; $d < 0$: falling terms; $d = 0$: all terms equal.
- To test a list, work out **every** difference; one equal pair is not enough.

*Example:* $-1.5, -4, -6.5, -9$ is an AP with $d = -2.5$; $2, 6, 18, 54$ is not an AP (differences $4, 12, 36$).

key_terms.definition_md: A sequence in which every term after the first is the previous term plus a fixed number $d$.
$d = T_{n+1} - T_n$, the same for every $n$.

visual.alt: Table of four sequences and their differences: 4, 11, 18, 25 has differences 7, 7, 7 and is an AP; 30, 24, 18, 12 has differences minus 6 each time and is an AP; 5, 5, 5, 5 has differences 0 and is an AP; 2, 3, 5, 8 has differences 1, 2, 3 and is not an AP.
visual.caption: Same difference every time: an AP. Changing differences: not an AP.

visuals.alt: Two arithmetic progressions plotted against term number: 2, 5.5, 9, 12.5, 16 rising by 3.5 each step, and 20, 17.5, 15, 12.5, 10 falling by 2.5 each step; both have 12.5 as their fourth term.
visuals.caption: Positive $d$: the terms rise. Negative $d$: they fall.

sections.heading: 2. The general (nth) term
sections.body_md:
Starting from the first term $a$, you add $d$ once for each step; the $n$th term is $n - 1$ steps after the first:

$$T_n = a + (n - 1)d$$

- $T_n$ is a linear expression in $n$: $T_n = dn + (a - d)$. Conversely, if $T_n = pn + q$, the sequence is an AP with $d = p$.
- Some books write $t_n$ or $a_n$ for the $n$th term.

*Example:* for $13, 8, 3, \ldots$: $T_n = 13 + (n - 1) \times (-5) = 18 - 5n$, so $T_{18} = -72$.

key_terms.definition_md: The $n$th term $T_n = a + (n - 1)d$, a formula for any term.

visual.alt: Table building the general term: term 1 is a, term 2 is a plus d, term 3 is a plus 2 d, term 4 is a plus 3 d, so term n is a plus n minus 1 times d; for 6, 10, 14 this gives 6, 10, 14, 18 and in general 4 n plus 2.
visual.caption: To reach the $n$th term you add $d$ exactly $n - 1$ times.

visuals.alt: Terms of 13, 8, 3 and so on plotted against n: the points lie on the falling line T n equals 18 minus 5 n, which reaches minus 72 at n equals 18.
visuals.caption: The $18$th term lies on the same line: $T_{18} = -72$.

sections.heading: 3. Which term? How many terms? Terms from the end
sections.body_md:
- **Is $v$ a term?** Solve $a + (n - 1)d = v$. It is a term only if $n$ is a **positive whole number**.
- **Number of terms** of a finite AP $a, \ldots, l$: solve $a + (n - 1)d = l$, i.e. $n = \dfrac{l - a}{d} + 1$.
- **From the end:** read backwards, the AP starts at $l$ with common difference $-d$, so the $m$th term from the end is $l - (m - 1)d$; it is also the $(n - m + 1)$th term from the start.

*Example:* $9, 16, \ldots, 352$ has $n = 50$ terms; the $10$th term from the end is $352 - 9 \times 7 = 289$, the $41$st term.

key_terms.definition_md: An AP with a last term $l$ and a definite number of terms $n$.
The $m$th term from the end is $l - (m - 1)d$.

nodes.label: No: it is not a term

visual.alt: Flow chart for deciding whether a number is a term: write a plus n minus 1 times d equal to the number, solve for n, and ask whether n is a positive whole number; if yes it is the nth term, if not it is not a term of the progression.
visual.caption: A term number must be a positive whole number.

visuals.alt: Table for the progression 9, 16, 23 up to 352: counted from the start the first three terms are 9, 16 and 23; counted from the end they are 352, 345 and 338; the mth term from the end is 352 minus m minus 1 times 7.
visuals.caption: Read backwards, an AP is still an AP, with common difference $-d$.

visuals.alt: The progression 9, 16, 23 up to 352 plotted against term number: a rising line from the point (1, 9) to the point (50, 352), with the 10th term from the end, 289, marked at n equals 41.
visuals.caption: The $10$th term from the end is the $50 - 10 + 1 = 41$st term.

sections.heading: 4. Finding an AP from conditions; three terms in AP
sections.body_md:
- **Two terms given** ($T_p$ and $T_q$): $T_q - T_p = (q - p)d$ gives $d$; then $a = T_p - (p - 1)d$.
- **Two other conditions** (sums of terms, a term and a sum): write each in $a$ and $d$ and solve the two linear equations.
- **Three unknown terms in AP:** take $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$ (sum $3a$).
- **Condition for three terms:** $a$, $b$, $c$ are in AP exactly when $2b = a + c$ ($b$ is the average of $a$ and $c$).

*Example:* $T_5 = 31$, $T_{14} = -5$: $9d = -36$, $d = -4$, $a = 47$.

key_terms.definition_md: Writing three terms as $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$ so that $d$ cancels in their sum.

rows: $a$, $b$, $c$ in AP exactly when $2b = a + c$

visual.alt: Table of two ideas for three terms in an arithmetic progression: write them as a minus d, a, a plus d so that their sum is 3 a; and a, b, c are in AP exactly when 2 b equals a plus c, which for 5 m plus 2, 4 m plus 7 and 2 m plus 15 gives m equals 3.
visual.caption: Symmetric terms make the sum simple.

visuals.alt: A falling line through the points (5, 31) and (14, minus 5), continued back to the first term 47 at n equals 1 and on to minus 69 at n equals 30.
visuals.caption: Two terms fix the line, and so the whole AP.

visuals.alt: Bar chart of the three numbers 7, 12 and 17: each bar is 5 taller than the one before, and the middle bar, 12, is the average of the other two.
visuals.caption: Equal steps of $5$ either side of the middle number $12$.

sections.heading: 5. Sum of the first n terms
sections.body_md:
Writing $S_n$ forwards and backwards and adding gives $n$ columns, each equal to $a + l$:

$$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + l) = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]$$

- Use $\dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]$ when $a$, $d$, $n$ are known; use $\dfrac{n}{2}(a + l)$ when the first and last terms are known.
- If only $a$, $d$ and $l$ are known, find $n$ first.
- Sum of a block of terms: $T_{m+1} + \cdots + T_n = S_n - S_m$.

*Example:* $-8 - 3 + 2 + \cdots + 112$: $n = 25$, so the sum is $\dfrac{25}{2}(-8 + 112) = 1300$.

visual.alt: Table writing the sum 4 plus 7 plus 10 plus 13 plus 16 plus 19 forwards and backwards: each column adds up to 23, so twice the sum is 6 times 23, which is 138, and the sum is 69.
visual.caption: Each column adds up to first term $+$ last term, so $S = \dfrac{6}{2}(4 + 19) = 69$.

visuals.alt: Flow chart for choosing a sum formula: if a, d and n are known use n over 2 times 2 a plus n minus 1 times d; if a, the last term l and n are known use n over 2 times a plus l; if a, d and l are known, first find n, then use n over 2 times a plus l.
visuals.caption: Two forms of the same formula.

visuals.alt: Running totals of 4, 7, 10, 13 and so on plotted against the number of terms: 4, 11, 21, 34, 50 and 69. The points lie on a curve that bends upwards, not on a straight line.
visuals.caption: The terms rise steadily, so the totals grow faster and faster.

visuals.alt: Bar chart of the first 30 terms of 6, 11, 16 and so on, in two colours: the first ten bars, from 6 to 51, and the next twenty bars, from 56 to 151, whose total is wanted.
visuals.caption: The wanted part is the whole $S_{30}$ minus the first part $S_{10}$.

sections.heading: 6. Finding n from a sum; terms from a sum rule
sections.body_md:
- **n from a given sum:** $\dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d] = S$ is a quadratic in $n$. Solve it and keep only **positive whole-number** roots; if both roots are valid, check the terms (a root may need a zero or negative "term", which a real problem may not allow).
- **Terms from a rule for $S_n$:** $T_1 = S_1$, and $T_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 2$.

*Example:* $25, 22, 19, \ldots$ with sum $116$: $3n^2 - 53n + 232 = 0$, so $n = 8$ (the root $\dfrac{29}{3}$ is rejected).

key_terms.definition_md: Discarding a solution of the quadratic that is negative, a fraction, or meaningless in the problem.

visual.alt: Graph of the sum of the first n terms of 25, 22, 19 and so on: it rises to just above 117 and falls again. The horizontal line at 116 meets it at n equals 8 and again at a fraction between 9 and 10, which is not a whole number of terms.
visual.caption: Only $n = 8$ is a whole number of terms; $n = \dfrac{29}{3}$ is rejected.

nodes.label: Set it equal to the given sum
Rearrange to a quadratic in $n$ and solve

visuals.alt: Flow chart for finding the number of terms from a given sum: write S n using a and d, set it equal to the sum, rearrange to a quadratic in n and solve, keep only positive whole-number roots, and check by working out the sum.
visuals.caption: A number of terms must be a positive whole number.

visuals.alt: Table for the sum rule S n equals 7 n minus n squared: the sums for n equals 1 to 5 are 6, 10, 12, 12 and 10, and the terms found by subtracting consecutive sums are 6, 4, 2, 0 and minus 2, an arithmetic progression with common difference minus 2.
visuals.caption: Subtracting consecutive sums gives the terms $6, 4, 2, 0, -2, \ldots$: $d = -2$.

sections.heading: 7. Applications
sections.body_md:
Quantities that change by a **fixed amount** each day, month, row or step form an AP: savings that grow by the same amount, instalments that rise or fall by the same amount, heights of stacks, temperatures on a climb, distances in successive seconds.

1. Identify $a$ (the first value), $d$ (the fixed change, with its sign) and what $n$ counts.
2. Decide whether a **term** (one value) or a **sum** (a total) is asked.
3. Watch the first term: if the first reading is at time $0$, the reading after $k$ steps is the $(k + 1)$th term.
4. Give the answer in words with units, and reject impossible values.

*Example:* a loan of ₹$30{,}000$ repaid by instalments $750, 900, 1050, \ldots$ needs $16$ instalments, the last being ₹$3{,}000$.

key_terms.definition_md: One of a series of payments; here each differs from the previous one by a fixed amount.

visual.alt: Bar chart of 16 monthly instalments rising by 150 rupees each month, from 750 rupees in month 1 to 3000 rupees in month 16; together they add up to 30000 rupees.
visual.caption: Sixteen instalments, each ₹$150$ more than the last, add up to ₹$30{,}000$.

visuals.alt: Height of a stack of imagined plastic chairs against the number of chairs: 82 centimetres for one chair, rising 4 centimetres per chair, 138 centimetres for 15 chairs and 150 centimetres for 18 chairs.
visuals.caption: Each extra chair adds the same $4$ cm.

visuals.alt: Total distance travelled by the imagined trolley against time: 4 centimetres after 1 second, 16 after 2 seconds, 36 after 3 seconds and 400 after 10 seconds, on the curve 4 n squared.
visuals.caption: Distances in each second form an AP; the running totals are $4n^2$.

visuals.alt: Table for choosing a method: a term from a, d and n uses a plus n minus 1 times d; which term solves that equal to the value; a sum uses either sum formula; the number of terms from a sum needs a quadratic in n; a term from a sum rule uses S n minus S n minus 1.
visuals.caption: Read the question for what is given and what is asked.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Find a term (2 marks):* $a$ and $d$ 1; term 1.
- *Is it a term / which term (2–3 marks):* equation 1; solving for $n$ 1; conclusion in words 1.
- *AP from two conditions (3–4 marks):* each equation 1; solving 1; the AP or the required term 1.
- *Sum (2–3 marks):* correct form of the formula 1; substitution and value 1–2.
- *Number of terms from a sum (4 marks):* equation 1; quadratic 1; roots 1; rejecting a root with a reason 1.
- *10-mark structured question:* parts (a), (b), (c), usually 3 + 3 + 4; show all working.

**Common mistakes**
1. Finding $d$ as $T_1 - T_2$ instead of $T_2 - T_1$.
2. Using $a + nd$ for the $n$th term, or $(n - 1)$ replaced by $n$ in the sum formula.
3. Forgetting the $\dfrac{n}{2}$ (or halving twice).
4. Accepting a negative or fractional number of terms.
5. Miscounting terms: $\dfrac{l - a}{d}$ counts the steps; add $1$ for the terms.
6. In applications, mixing units (m and cm) or taking the reading at time $0$ as the first step.

questions.stem_md: Only one of these sequences has the same difference between every pair of consecutive terms. Which one is an arithmetic progression?
questions.solution_md: In (a) each term is $0.7$ more than the one before: $3.1 - 2.4 = 3.8 - 3.1 = 4.5 - 3.8 = 0.7$. In (b) the differences are $3, 6, 12$; in (c) they are $3, 5, 7$; in (d) they are $-2, -3, -4$. None of these is constant.

questions.stem_md: What is the common difference of the AP $-7, -3.5, 0, 3.5, \ldots$?
questions.solution_md: $d = T_2 - T_1 = -3.5 - (-7) = 3.5$. Option (c) subtracts the wrong way round, (d) adds the first two terms, and (a) is the difference between alternate terms.

questions.stem_md: The $21$st term of the AP $9, 5.5, 2, \ldots$ is
questions.solution_md: $a = 9$ and $d = 5.5 - 9 = -3.5$, so $T_{21} = 9 + 20 \times (-3.5) = 9 - 70 = -61$. Option (d) uses $21d$ instead of $20d$, (a) uses $d = +3.5$, and (b) is the $20$th term.

questions.stem_md: Which expression gives the $n$th term of the AP $5, 12, 19, 26, \ldots$?
questions.solution_md: $T_n = a + (n - 1)d = 5 + (n - 1) \times 7 = 7n - 2$. Check: $T_1 = 7 - 2 = 5$. Option (b) is $a + nd$, which would make the first term $12$.

questions.stem_md: Starting from $15$ and adding $6$ each time gives the AP $15, 21, 27, \ldots$ In which position does $171$ appear?
questions.solution_md: $15 + (n - 1) \times 6 = 171 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times 6 = 156 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 26 \Rightarrow n = 27$. Option (b) forgets to add $1$: $n - 1$ counts the steps from the first term, not the terms.

questions.stem_md: How many terms are there in the AP $101, 97, 93, \ldots, -27$?
questions.solution_md: $d = -4$. If $-27$ is the $n$th term, $101 + (n - 1) \times (-4) = -27 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times (-4) = -128 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 32 \Rightarrow n = 33$. Option (c) counts the steps between the first and last terms, not the terms.

questions.stem_md: In an AP, $T_4 = -2$ and $T_9 = 18$. What is the common difference?
questions.solution_md: $T_9 - T_4 = (a + 8d) - (a + 3d) = 5d$, so $5d = 18 - (-2) = 20 \Rightarrow d = 4$. Option (d) uses $18 - 2$ instead of $18 - (-2)$, and (a) divides by $4$ instead of $5$.

questions.stem_md: What is the $6$th term from the end of the AP $3, 10, 17, \ldots, 136$?
questions.solution_md: Read the AP backwards: it starts at $l = 136$ and has common difference $-7$. So the $6$th term from the end is $136 + 5 \times (-7) = 136 - 35 = 101$. Option (a) takes $6$ steps instead of $5$, and (b) is the $6$th term from the start.

questions.stem_md: Three numbers in AP add up to $24$, and the largest of them is $14$. What is the smallest?
questions.solution_md: Take the numbers as $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$. Then $(a - d) + a + (a + d) = 3a = 24$, so $a = 8$. The largest gives $8 + d = 14 \Rightarrow d = 6$, and the smallest is $8 - 6 = 2$.

questions.stem_md: What do the first $18$ terms of the AP $-5, -1, 3, \ldots$ add up to?
questions.solution_md: $a = -5$, $d = 4$: $S_{18} = \dfrac{18}{2}[2 \times (-5) + 17 \times 4] = 9 \times (-10 + 68) = 9 \times 58 = 522$. Option (c) uses $18d$ instead of $17d$, and (d) forgets to halve.

questions.stem_md: What is the value of $12 + 19 + 26 + \cdots + 145$?
questions.solution_md: $d = 7$. Number of terms: $12 + (n - 1) \times 7 = 145 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 19 \Rightarrow n = 20$. So $S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}(12 + 145) = 10 \times 157 = 1570$. Option (d) takes $n = 19$, the number of steps, and (a) forgets to halve.

questions.stem_md: The sum of the first $n$ terms of an AP is given by $S_n = 4n^2 - n$. Find its common difference.
The terms of the AP $5, 8, 11, \ldots$ are added one after another. After how many terms does the running total reach exactly $258$?
questions.solution_md: $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[10 + (n - 1) \times 3] = \dfrac{n(3n + 7)}{2}$. Setting $\dfrac{n(3n + 7)}{2} = 258$: $3n^2 + 7n - 516 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 12)(3n + 43) = 0 \Rightarrow n = 12 \text{ or } n = -\dfrac{43}{3}$. A number of terms cannot be negative, so $n = 12$.

questions.stem_md: Adding every multiple of $5$ from $5$ up to $100$ gives
questions.solution_md: The multiples $5, 10, 15, \ldots, 100$ form an AP with $a = 5$, $d = 5$ and $n = 20$ terms. $S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}(5 + 100) = 10 \times 105 = 1050$. Option (c) forgets to halve.

questions.stem_md: An AP has $n$ terms; its first term is $a$ and its last term is $l$. Which expression gives the sum of all its terms?
questions.solution_md: Pair the first term with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on: each pair adds up to $a + l$, and there are $\dfrac{n}{2}$ pairs. For example, $4 + 7 + 10 + 13 = 34$ and $\dfrac{4}{2}(4 + 13) = 34$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined pottery workshop in Khurja makes $18$ pots on its first day and, on every later day, $3$ more pots than on the day before. How many pots does it make on day $15$?
questions.solution_md: The daily numbers form an AP with $a = 18$ and $d = 3$, so on day $15$: $T_{15} = 18 + 14 \times 3 = 60$. Option (a) adds $15 \times 3$ instead of $14 \times 3$, and (b) is the number for day $14$.

questions.stem_md: An imagined candle is $24$ cm tall when it is lit and burns down by $1.5$ cm every hour, so its heights at the start and after each hour form an AP. After how many hours is it $6$ cm tall?
questions.solution_md: The heights are $24, 22.5, 21, \ldots$ with $a = 24$ and $d = -1.5$. If $6$ is the $n$th height, $24 + (n - 1) \times (-1.5) = 6 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 12 \Rightarrow n = 13$. The first height is measured at $0$ hours, so the $13$th is measured after $12$ hours. Option (b) gives the term number instead of the number of hours.

questions.stem_md: An imagined school library charges a late fine that grows each day: ₹$3$ for the first day, ₹$5$ for the second, ₹$7$ for the third, and so on. Kabir returns a book $12$ days late. What is his total fine?
questions.solution_md: The daily fines form an AP with $a = 3$, $d = 2$ and $n = 12$: $S_{12} = \dfrac{12}{2}[2 \times 3 + 11 \times 2] = 6 \times 28 = 168$, so the fine is ₹$168$. Option (c) is only the fine for day $12$, and (d) is $12 \times 25$, which forgets to halve.

questions.stem_md: An AP has last term $l$ and common difference $d$. Which expression gives its $10$th term counted from the end?
questions.solution_md: Counting backwards from $l$, each step subtracts $d$, and the $10$th term from the end is $9$ steps back: $l - 9d$. Option (b) is the $10$th term from the start.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sequence with $n$th term $T_n = 9 - 4n$ is an AP with common difference $-4$.

**Reason (R):** If the $n$th term of a sequence is $pn + q$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants, the sequence is an AP with common difference $p$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $T_{n+1} - T_n = [9 - 4(n + 1)] - (9 - 4n) = -4$ for every $n$; the terms are $5, 1, -3, \ldots$, so A is true. R is true in general, because the difference between consecutive terms is $p(n + 1) + q - (pn + q) = p$; A is the case $p = -4$, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For the progression $1.5, 4, 6.5, \ldots$, the value of $T_{15}$ is $36.5$.

**Reason (R):** To get the $n$th term of an AP, add $n$ copies of the common difference $d$ to the first term $a$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $T_{15} = 1.5 + 14 \times 2.5 = 1.5 + 35 = 36.5$, so A is true. R is false: the $n$th term is $a + (n - 1)d$, because there are only $n - 1$ steps from the first term to the $n$th. (Using R would give $1.5 + 15 \times 2.5 = 39$.)

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sum of the first $10$ terms of the AP $20, 17, 14, \ldots$ is $65$.

**Reason (R):** An AP whose common difference is negative eventually has negative terms.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: $S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}[2 \times 20 + 9 \times (-3)] = 5 \times 13 = 65$, so A is true. R is also true (here $T_8 = 20 + 7 \times (-3) = -1$), but it is not the reason for A, which follows from the sum formula.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** $300$ is a term of the AP $5, 13, 21, \ldots$

**Reason (R):** Every term of the AP $5, 13, 21, \ldots$ leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by $8$.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: R is true: each term is $5 + 8(n - 1)$, a multiple of $8$ plus $5$. But $300 = 8 \times 37 + 4$ leaves remainder $4$, so $300$ is not a term; equivalently, $5 + (n - 1) \times 8 = 300$ gives $n - 1 = 36.875$, since $36.875 \times 8 = 295$. A is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** For an AP with $S_5 = 40$ and $S_6 = 51$, the $6$th term is $11$.

**Reason (R):** In any AP, the difference $T_6 - T_5$ equals the common difference.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation for (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation for (A).

questions.solution_md: The $6$th term is what the sixth addition contributes: $T_6 = S_6 - S_5 = 51 - 40 = 11$, so A is true. R is also true, but A uses $T_n = S_n - S_{n-1}$, not the common difference, so R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md: If the same number is subtracted from every term of an AP, the result is again an AP with the same common difference.

questions.stem_md: The $4$th term of an AP is $9$, and the sum of its $6$th and $13$th terms is $40$. Find the AP.

answer.model_answer_md:

From the first equation, $a = 9 - 3d$. Substituting in the second: $2(9 - 3d) + 17d = 40 \Rightarrow 18 + 11d = 40 \Rightarrow d = 2$.

Then $a = 9 - 3 \times 2 = 3$, and the AP is $3, 5, 7, 9, \ldots$

questions.stem_md: The sum of three numbers in AP is $30$ and the sum of their squares is $332$. Find the numbers.

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the numbers be $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$. Their sum is $3a = 30$, so $a = 10$.

Sum of squares: $(10 - d)^2 + 10^2 + (10 + d)^2 = 300 + 2d^2 = 332 \Rightarrow 2d^2 = 32 \Rightarrow d^2 = 16 \Rightarrow d = 4 \text{ or } d = -4$.

So the numbers are $6, 10, 14$ (with $d = -4$ they are the same numbers in the order $14, 10, 6$).

questions.stem_md:

questions.stem_md:
An imagined bakery in Mumbai bakes $120$ buns on its first day of business, and on each later day it bakes $8$ more buns than on the day before.

(a) How many buns does it bake on day $25$?

(b) How many buns does it bake in its first $25$ days altogether?

answer.model_answer_md:
The daily numbers form an AP with $a = 120$ and $d = 8$.

**(a)** $T_{25} = 120 + 24 \times 8 = 312$ buns.

**(b)** $S_{25} = \dfrac{25}{2}(120 + 312) = 12.5 \times 432 = 5400$ buns.

questions.stem_md: The sum of the $4$th and $8$th terms of an AP is $24$, and the sum of its $6$th and $10$th terms is $44$. Find the first three terms of the AP.

answer.model_answer_md:
$T_4 + T_8 = (a + 3d) + (a + 7d) = 2a + 10d = 24$.

$T_6 + T_{10} = (a + 5d) + (a + 9d) = 2a + 14d = 44$.

Subtracting the first equation from the second: $4d = 20 \Rightarrow d = 5$. Then $2a + 50 = 24 \Rightarrow a = -13$.

The first three terms are $-13, -8, -3$.

questions.stem_md: Which term of the AP $8, 14.5, 21, \ldots$ exceeds its $12$th term by $117$?

answer.model_answer_md:
$a = 8$, $d = 6.5$, and $T_{12} = 8 + 11 \times 6.5 = 79.5$.

The required term is $79.5 + 117 = 196.5$.

$8 + (n - 1) \times 6.5 = 196.5 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times 6.5 = 188.5 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 29 \Rightarrow n = 30$.

So the $30$th term exceeds the $12$th by $117$. (Quicker: $117 \div 6.5 = 18$ steps after the $12$th term, and $12 + 18 = 30$.)

questions.solution_md: Find the 12th term, add 117, then find which term has that value.

questions.stem_md: The sum of the first $8$ terms of an AP is $88$, and the sum of its next $8$ terms (the $9$th to the $16$th) is $344$. Find the first term and the common difference.

answer.model_answer_md:
$S_8 = \dfrac{8}{2}(2a + 7d) = 88 \Rightarrow 2a + 7d = 22$.

The first $16$ terms add up to $S_{16} = 88 + 344 = 432$, and $S_{16} = \dfrac{16}{2}(2a + 15d) = 432 \Rightarrow 2a + 15d = 54$.

Subtracting: $8d = 32 \Rightarrow d = 4$; then $2a + 28 = 22 \Rightarrow a = -3$.

Check: the AP is $-3, 1, 5, \ldots$ and $S_8 = 4(-6 + 28) = 88$.

questions.solution_md: The next eight terms add to S₁₆ − S₈, so S₁₆ is known; the two sum formulas give two linear equations in a and d.

questions.stem_md: How many terms of the AP $-14, -10, -6, \ldots$ must be added to give a sum of $40$? Explain why the sum is negative when only the first few terms are added.

answer.model_answer_md:
$a = -14$, $d = 4$: $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[-28 + (n - 1) \times 4] = 2n^2 - 16n$.

$2n^2 - 16n = 40 \Rightarrow n^2 - 8n - 20 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 10)(n + 2) = 0 \Rightarrow n = 10 \text{ or } n = -2$.

A number of terms cannot be negative, so $n = 10$. Check: $T_{10} = -14 + 9 \times 4 = 22$ and $S_{10} = 5(-14 + 22) = 40$.

The first four terms $-14, -10, -6, -2$ are negative, so the running total falls at first ($S_4 = -32$); it becomes positive only when the positive terms outweigh them, from $n = 9$ on ($S_9 = 18$).

questions.solution_md: Write S_n as a quadratic in n, set it equal to 40, solve and reject the negative root; look at the signs of the early terms for the explanation.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined nursery in Shimla plants a cedar sapling that is $35$ cm tall, and the sapling grows $2.5$ cm every week.

(a) Show that its heights at planting and at the end of each week form an AP.

(b) Find its height at the end of the $20$th week.

(c) At the end of which week will it first be $1$ m tall?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The heights $35, 37.5, 40, \ldots$ (in cm) go up by the same $2.5$ cm each week, so they form an AP with $a = 35$ and $d = 2.5$.

**(b)** The height at the end of week $w$ is the $(w + 1)$th term. After $20$ weeks: $T_{21} = 35 + 20 \times 2.5 = 85$ cm.

**(c)** $1$ m is $100$ cm: $35 + (n - 1) \times 2.5 = 100 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times 2.5 = 65 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 26 \Rightarrow n = 27$.

The $27$th height is the one at the end of week $26$, so the sapling is first $1$ m tall at the end of the $26$th week.

questions.solution_md: The first height is at week 0, so the height after w weeks is term number w + 1; keep the units the same (100 cm).

questions.stem_md:

(b) How many tickets does it sell for its first $12$ shows altogether?

(c) Which is the first show to sell fewer than $30$ tickets?

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** $S_{12} = \dfrac{12}{2}[300 + 11 \times (-12)] = 6 \times 168 = 1008$ tickets.

**(c)** $T_{11} = 150 - 120 = 30$ and $T_{12} = 150 - 132 = 18 < 30$, so the $12$th show is the first to sell fewer than $30$ tickets.

(b) Write the $n$th term of this AP, and find its $25$th term.

(c) Is $150$ a term of this AP? Which term of the AP is $187$?

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** $T_n = -1 + (n - 1) \times 4 = 4n - 5$, and $T_{25} = 4 \times 25 - 5 = 95$.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) How many terms are there in the AP $120, 114.5, 109, \ldots, -12$?

(b) Find the $8$th term from the end of this AP.

(c) Three numbers in AP have a sum of $21$ and a product of $231$. Find the numbers.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $d = -5.5$. If $-12$ is the $n$th term, $120 + (n - 1) \times (-5.5) = -12 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times (-5.5) = -132 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 24 \Rightarrow n = 25$.

**(b)** Read backwards, the AP starts at $-12$ with common difference $5.5$, so the $8$th term from the end is $-12 + 7 \times 5.5 = 26.5$. (Check: it is the $25 - 8 + 1 = 18$th term, and $T_{18} = 120 + 17 \times (-5.5) = 26.5$.)

**(c)** Let the numbers be $a - d$, $a$, $a + d$. Their sum is $3a = 21$, so $3a = 21 \Rightarrow a = 7$.

Product: $(7 - d) \times 7 \times (7 + d) = 7(49 - d^2) = 231$, so $49 - d^2 = 33 \Rightarrow d^2 = 16 \Rightarrow d = 4 \text{ or } d = -4$.

The numbers are $3, 7, 11$ (or $11, 7, 3$). Check: $3 + 7 + 11 = 21$ and $3 \times 7 \times 11 = 231$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) solves a + (n − 1)d = −12; part (b) reverses the AP (or uses term n − 8 + 1); part (c) takes the numbers as a − d, a, a + d.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) Find the sum of the first $18$ terms of the AP $15, 11, 7, \ldots$

(b) How many terms of the AP $6, 10, 14, \ldots$ must be added to get $198$?

(c) The sum of the first $n$ terms of an AP is $S_n = \dfrac{3n^2 + 13n}{2}$. Find the AP and its $20$th term.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $a = 15$, $d = -4$: $S_{18} = \dfrac{18}{2}[2 \times 15 + 17 \times (-4)] = 9 \times (30 - 68) = 9 \times (-38) = -342$.

**(b)** $a = 6$, $d = 4$: $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[12 + (n - 1) \times 4] = n(2n + 4) = 2n^2 + 4n$.

$2n^2 + 4n = 198 \Rightarrow n^2 + 2n - 99 = 0 \Rightarrow (n + 11)(n - 9) = 0 \Rightarrow n = 9 \text{ or } n = -11$. A number of terms cannot be negative, so $9$ terms are needed.

**(c)** $T_1 = S_1 = \dfrac{3 + 13}{2} = 8$ and $S_2 = \dfrac{12 + 26}{2} = 19$, so $T_2 = S_2 - S_1 = 19 - 8 = 11$ and $d = 11 - 8 = 3$.

The AP is $8, 11, 14, \ldots$ and $T_{20} = 8 + 19 \times 3 = 65$.

questions.solution_md: Part (a) is the sum formula with a negative d; part (b) sets S_n = 198 and solves a quadratic; part (c) uses T₁ = S₁ and T₂ = S₂ − S₁.

questions.stem_md:
Ananya, an imagined Class 10 student in Guwahati, saves ₹$120$ in January, ₹$135$ in February, ₹$150$ in March, and so on: each month she saves ₹$15$ more than in the month before. Show all working.

(a) How much does she save in December of the same year?

(b) How much does she save in the whole year, January to December?

(c) She keeps saving in the same way. After how many months will her total savings be exactly ₹$3{,}720$?

answer.model_answer_md:
Her monthly savings form an AP with $a = 120$ and $d = 15$.

**(a)** December is the $12$th month: $T_{12} = 120 + 11 \times 15 = 285$, so she saves ₹$285$.

**(b)** $S_{12} = \dfrac{12}{2}(120 + 285) = 6 \times 405 = 2430$, so she saves ₹$2{,}430$ in the year.

**(c)** $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[240 + (n - 1) \times 15] = \dfrac{n(15n + 225)}{2}$.

$\dfrac{n(15n + 225)}{2} = 3720 \Rightarrow 15n^2 + 225n - 7440 = 0 \Rightarrow n^2 + 15n - 496 = 0$.

$(n - 16)(n + 31) = 0 \Rightarrow n = 16 \text{ or } n = -31$.

A number of months cannot be negative, so her total reaches ₹$3{,}720$ after $16$ months, that is, at the end of April of the following year.

questions.solution_md: Parts (a) and (b) use the nth-term and sum formulas with n = 12; part (c) sets S_n equal to the target, solves the quadratic and interprets the positive root as a month.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined self-help group lends ₹$63{,}000$ to a family, free of interest. The family repays it in monthly instalments: ₹$5{,}000$ in the first month, and each later instalment is ₹$200$ less than the one before. Show all working.

(a) Find the $10$th instalment.

(b) Find the total repaid in the first $10$ months.

(c) How many instalments repay the loan exactly, and what is the last instalment? Explain why one root of your equation must be rejected.

answer.model_answer_md:
The instalments form an AP with $a = 5000$ and $d = -200$.

**(a)** $T_{10} = 5000 + 9 \times (-200) = 3200$: the $10$th instalment is ₹$3{,}200$.

**(b)** $S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}(5000 + 3200) = 5 \times 8200 = 41000$: ₹$41{,}000$ is repaid in the first $10$ months.

**(c)** $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[10000 + (n - 1) \times (-200)] = n(5100 - 100n)$.

$n(5100 - 100n) = 63000 \Rightarrow n^2 - 51n + 630 = 0 \Rightarrow (n - 21)(n - 30) = 0 \Rightarrow n = 21 \text{ or } n = 30$.

Now $T_{21} = 5000 + 20 \times (-200) = 1000$ but $T_{30} = 5000 + 29 \times (-200) = -800$. An instalment cannot be negative (the instalments after the $25$th would be zero or less), so $n = 30$ is rejected.

The loan is repaid in $21$ instalments, and the last instalment is ₹$1{,}000$.

questions.solution_md: Parts (a) and (b) use the term and sum formulas for a falling AP; in part (c) both roots of the quadratic are positive, so check the last instalment for each.

questions.stem_md:
On an imagined trek in Sikkim, the temperature at the base camp is $18$ °C, and it falls by $1.5$ °C for every $250$ m climbed. A hiker records the temperature at the base camp and then after every $250$ m of climbing. Show all working.

(a) Show that the readings form an AP, and find the temperature after climbing $2$ km.

(b) How high above the base camp is the temperature $-3$ °C?

(c) The hiker records $13$ readings in all, the last one after $3$ km. Find the sum of the readings, and hence their average.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Each reading is $1.5$ °C lower than the one before, so the readings $18, 16.5, 15, \ldots$ form an AP with $a = 18$ and $d = -1.5$.

$2$ km $= 2000$ m and $2000 \div 250 = 8$ climbs of $250$ m, so the temperature is the $9$th reading: $T_9 = 18 + 8 \times (-1.5) = 6$ °C.

**(b)** $18 + (n - 1) \times (-1.5) = -3 \Rightarrow (n - 1) \times (-1.5) = -21 \Rightarrow n - 1 = 14$: that is $14$ climbs of $250$ m, and $14 \times 250 = 3500$, so it is $-3$ °C at $3500$ m (3.5 km) above the base camp.

**(c)** $T_{13} = 18 + 12 \times (-1.5) = 0$ °C, so $S_{13} = \dfrac{13}{2}(18 + 0) = 117$.

Average: $117 \div 13 = 9$ °C.

questions.solution_md: The first reading is at 0 m, so the reading after k climbs is term k + 1; the sum of the readings divided by their number gives the average.

questions.stem_md:
Answer each part. Show all working.

(a) The $5$th term of an AP is $26$, and the sum of its first $5$ terms is $90$. Find the first term and the common difference.

(b) Find the sum of the first $20$ terms of this AP.

(c) Find the sum of its terms from the $21$st to the $40$th in two ways: as $S_{40} - S_{20}$, and by using the first and last of those terms.

**(b)** $S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2}[20 + 19 \times 4] = 10 \times 96 = 960$.

**(c)** First way: $S_{40} = \dfrac{40}{2}[20 + 39 \times 4] = 20 \times 176 = 3520$, so $S_{40} - S_{20} = 3520 - 960 = 2560$.

Second way: there are $20$ terms from the $21$st to the $40$th; $T_{21} = 10 + 20 \times 4 = 90$ and $T_{40} = 10 + 39 \times 4 = 166$, so their sum is $\dfrac{20}{2}(90 + 166) = 10 \times 256 = 2560$. Both ways give $2560$.
